name: Sara Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Sara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, which is an independent research group. We're not connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential. Would you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm Sara, 58, and I lead a construction crew that builds new lines for the electricity company, mostly connecting the solar and wind farms out on the plains to the main grid. Before that I spent twenty years on ordinary repair work in town. My husband Emre teaches maths at the secondary school, our son Deniz is 30 and works as a nurse in another city, and our daughter Aylin is 25, back home, studying graphic design.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Long drives, big skies, and a lot of mud. We set new poles or steel structures, pull in the wire, and hook up a new solar farm's substation, which is the yard of equipment that steps the voltage up for the grid. I'm the one on the crew who flies the drone to check the stringing and who feeds the site photos into an AI tool to catch problems early, I use it every day. What I love is seeing a field of nothing turn into power by the end of the season. What wears me out is the waiting, for permits, for parts, for landowners to sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'Good, now can we get it to sort out the permit backlog?' Honestly, I'd shrug. It does some useful things and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes. We're building out solar and wind for years either way, so the work's there. I'd retire around 62 or 63 and maybe do some consulting for contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do. Use the tools that help, drop the ones that don't. We've got about four months of bills saved, and we'd keep topping it up, maybe help Aylin a bit while she finishes her course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the hype, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use the AI tools on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I take drone photos of the stringing and the tool flags a sag or a bad clamp. I also use a chatbot to write the daily site report and to check the specs on parts against the drawings. It saves me maybe an hour a day, which I spend arguing with suppliers instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your last working years look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend it training my crew on the drone and the tools so they don't need me. Maybe a bit of consulting after, a few days a month. And Emre and I want to walk the long coastal trail when we both stop.

S0.say: She'd shrug and say AI does some useful things and that's that, joking that it should now be put to work on the permit backlog.
S0.think: Not much changes for her, since the solar and wind build-out means years of work either way. She'd retire around 62 or 63 and maybe consult for contractors.
S0.do: Keeps using the tools that help and drops the ones that don't. Keeps topping up savings of about four months of bills and helps her daughter Aylin while she finishes her course.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit bored by the hype.
S0.quote: It saves me maybe an hour a day, which I spend arguing with suppliers instead.
S0.fieldNote: Sara is the crew's tech person and uses AI daily for drone photo checks and site reports. She's pragmatic and unexcited either way. Her work connecting renewable farms gives her a strong sense that demand for line building isn't going away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any big change: some jobs go, some appear, and the people who learn fastest do best. I'd say the company should train everyone, and people should take the training. I'd post about the useful tools in our crew group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's good for me. I'm already the one using this stuff, and companies will want leads who can run a crew with new kit. I'd be busier, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to let my crew trial whatever new tools come out first, from month one. I'd take a course on the automated stringing equipment if it showed up. And I'd sit down with Aylin about her design course, because that's the kind of work that might shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your family or crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aylin, more than anyone. She draws beautifully, but the AI image tools are already doing what she's training for. And on the crew, Gary, who's 60 and still writes everything in a little notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want to bring in more automation on your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it makes the work safer or faster. Things like machines that set poles or pull wire without someone standing underneath. I'd want to be the one testing them, not the one reading about them.

S1.say: She'd say it's like any big change: some jobs go, some appear, and the fastest learners do best. The company should train everyone and people should take the training, and she'd post about useful tools in her crew group.
S1.think: She thinks it's good for her, since she already uses this kind of tool and companies will want crew leads who can run new kit. She'd be busier, if anything.
S1.do: Asks for her crew to trial new tools from the first month and takes a course on automated stringing equipment if it appears. Sits down with Aylin to talk about her design course.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the one testing them, not the one reading about them.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change suits her, and she'd volunteer her crew as the test bed. Her real worry is her daughter's design studies, not her own job. Her centre outlook shows in splitting the duty between the company training people and people taking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's be practical. Even if the AI is ready in two years, the grid isn't, someone still has to build, certify and connect it. I'd tell people to learn the new kit and not to waste energy panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right, but the house wouldn't. Emre's teaching might change a lot, Aylin's field could disappear, and that's two out of three adults in our home. My own job I'm less worried about, strangely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push to run the company's first robot crew trial, starting in the first few months. I'd put a bit more into savings and stop the plan for a new car. And I'd look at starting a small sideline, training other crews on drones and the new kit, because there'll be a rush for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More worried for them than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your own job worries you less. Why, when you’d be 60 and the change is so fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the work I do takes years to build and permit. You can't just drop a robot in a field and have a substation by Friday. In two years I'd be running robots, not replaced by them, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Aylin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to keep drawing, but to learn the tools too, every one of them. And I'd tell her she can stay home as long as she needs. She's our daughter, not a lodger.

S2.say: She'd say be practical: even if the AI is ready in two years, the grid isn't, and someone still has to build, certify and connect it. She'd tell people to learn the new kit and not waste energy panicking.
S2.think: She thinks she'd be all right but her household wouldn't, as Emre's teaching might change a lot and Aylin's field could disappear. She's strangely less worried about her own job.
S2.do: Pushes to run the company's first robot crew trial within months, saves a bit more and drops the plan for a new car. Starts a sideline training other crews on drones and new equipment.
S2.feel: Uneasy, more worried for her family than for herself.
S2.quote: You can't just drop a robot in a field and have a substation by Friday.
S2.fieldNote: Her calm comes from a practical belief that building and permitting the grid takes years whatever the AI can do. Her worry moves to her husband and daughter. She'd move toward the change by running the robot trial and training others as a sideline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if we start now. Companies should be training crews and governments should make the rules clear, so nobody's left guessing. I'd be telling the young ones to get their drone and robot certificates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think this one's actually quite good. I'd have time to become the person who runs robot crews, then retire on my own timing. The family has time to adjust too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get certified on whatever robot equipment is coming, and offer to write the training for our district. I'd start the training sideline on weekends to test whether it pays. Emre and I would also help Aylin move to a course with more of a future, maybe user design or something hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what's the first step you'd take this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the next course at the trade college that covers automated line equipment. And I'd ask my manager, straight out, who's going to lead the robot pilots, and tell him it should be me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd be sad to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being up there, honestly. The view from a new tower on a cold morning, when the wire's just gone in. Supervising robots from a truck isn't the same, but at 63 my knees will probably thank me.

S3.say: She'd say five years is plenty if work starts now, with companies training crews and governments making the rules clear. She'd tell young workers to get drone and robot certificates now.
S3.think: She thinks this one is quite good for her, with time to become the person who runs robot crews and then retire when she chooses. The family has time to adjust too.
S3.do: Gets certified on the coming robot equipment, offers to write district training and tests a weekend training sideline. Helps Aylin move to a course with more of a future.
S3.quote: Supervising robots from a truck isn't the same, but at 63 my knees will probably thank me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is her sweet spot: enough time to lead the change at work and steer her daughter's studies. She'd ask her manager directly for the robot pilot role. Her only real loss is the view from the tower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse for anyone not to get ready. I'd say companies, governments and people all have time to do their part. It's not a crisis, it's a project.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'll be 68, retired, maybe doing a bit of consulting or training. The question is just how much I want to be part of it before I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as now, keep using the tools, and in a few years take on training the crews on robots. I'd build up the consulting idea slowly so it's ready for when I retire. Keep saving steadily, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, mainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put any money into this, or into your own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We might put a little into a fund that covers robotics and the grid, nothing big, we don't have big. Mostly I'd invest in my own certificates. That's the best return I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Deniz?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nursing is people work, so I think he's fine for longer than most. I'd tell him to learn the tools anyway, because the hospital will change too. And to come home more often, while I'm still young enough to take him for a long walk.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse for anyone not to get ready. Companies, governments and people all have time to do their part, and it's a project, not a crisis.
S4.think: It's fine for her: she'll be 68 and retired, maybe consulting or training. The only question is how much she wants to be part of it before she stops.
S4.do: Carries on using the tools and in a few years takes on training crews on robots. Builds the consulting idea slowly for retirement and might put a small amount into a robotics and grid fund.
S4.quote: It's not a crisis, it's a project.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes her entirely relaxed and she frames it as a project to manage. She'd build her consulting sideline and put a little money into a fund, while calling her own certificates the best investment. Her son's nursing feels safe to her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, but for my family more than for me. Emre and Aylin would get hit first. What would help is good, quick retraining that people can actually afford, and honest information about which fields are safe, so a 25-year-old isn't spending three years on a course that won't exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: What it takes to build the grid all this needs. Everyone talks about AI like it's floating in the air, but every one of those computers runs on power from a line someone like me built. The robots will need us before they replace us.

headlineQuote: The robots will need us before they replace us.
portrait: Sara Yilmaz is a 58-year-old crew lead building new lines that connect solar and wind farms to the grid, and the person on her crew who flies the drone and uses AI every day. She's calm through the plateau and steady disruption, and even with AGI by 2028 she's only uneasy, because she believes the grid itself takes years to build and someone has to run the robots. Her real worry is her household, especially her husband Emre's teaching and her daughter Aylin's design studies. With five or ten years she sees a project to lead: robot certificates, training others as a sideline and some consulting into retirement.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, mainly because her husband and daughter would be hit before she would.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, affordable retraining and honest information about which fields are safe, so young people don't train for jobs that won't exist.
